newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Hughes hopeful of jobs chapter in new EU treaty.
newsitem.headline: Hughes hopeful of jobs chapter in new EU treaty.

text.p: The newly re-elected head of the European Parliament's employment and social affairs committee said on Wednesday he was hopeful the EU would soon have specific powers to tackle unemployment.
"Our great hope is that the inter-governmental conference (on reform of the European Union treaty) will give us a jobs chapter," Stephen Hughes told Reuters in an interview.
Other crucial concerns for the committee were effective reform of the European Structural Funds and a British decision to sign up to the social chapter, the British Socialist said.
Fourteen of the EU's 15 member states agreed on the need to give the EU specific competence to combat unemployment, though they had yet to agree on the form this might take, Hughes said.
Only Britain totally opposed including a jobs chapter in the treaty, he said, at a time when "true estimates" put the number of jobless in the EU at 27 million.
Hughes said he would be happy with the formula proposed by Ireland, which would allow the EU a greater role in coordinating job-creating efforts.
Work on reform of the European Structural Funds will be another priority for the employment and social affairs committee between now and the end of the current parliamentary term in June 1999.
"There seems to be an obsession with locations -- which areas are eligible for funding -- rather than (asking) where does the money best need to be targeted for unemployment reducing," Hughes said.

In future the structural fund arrangements needed to be more flexible and respond better to the specific problems facing individual sectors, such as helping small and medium-sized enterprises to take advantage of new information and communications technology, he said.

But he feared attempts at reform would provoke a fierce turf battle within the European Commission, with each service fearful they would lose control of structural fund money to the regional policy directorate (DG XVI).
Echoing Detlev Samland, the head of parliament's budget committee, Hughes said the problem of underspending in the structural funds also needed tackling.
He saw three reasons for this.
The member states were hidebound by bureaucratic problems and Britain had declined to use EU funding available for the job initiatives "Employment" and "Adapt" to make a political point.

In addition, in their drive to reduce public spending in the run up to the EU single currency, the member states preferred not to take up structural fund money, which they had to match penny for penny, but to wait until the money was returned to them in rebates from the EU budget.
This was understandable to a certain extent, Hughes said, stressing the importance of economic and monetary union, but it was misguided.
"If we are to succeed as a European Union we have to subscribe to the idea that cohesion is important and that use of the structural funds is an important way of achieving it," he said.

Hughes, who has been a Euro-MP for the last 13 years, said the employment and social affairs committee was unanimous in wanting Britain to sign up to the EU's social protocol, which is supported by all other member states.
He denied this would lead to a surge in new EU legislation because the Union had already adopted most of the necessary social measures at the introduction of the internal market.

In Hughes's mind, the only major areas where new EU social legislation is needed concern the rights of part time workers and temporary workers, portability of pensions from one member state to another and worker consultation.

The committee chairman said he agreed with industry that the future lay in more flexible patterns of work but insisted the casualisation of labour had to go hand in hand with proper social protection.
If people had security, they would be more likely to embrace change rather than resist it, he said.
They needed to know they would receive adequate pay, pensions and holidays if they worked part time, and the chance to retrain.
Frightening statistics showed only eight percent of jobless people were retraining at any one time, Hughes said.
"That leads 92 percent off into a delearning cul de sac at a time when technology is changing rapidly," he warned.
Hughes was confident that if the British Labour Party won the general election in Britain this spring, it would sign up to the social chapter as soon as possible.
The alternative, he predicted, would be a two-speed Europe which would backfire on Britain.
The other member states would not look favourably on British attempts to gain "an unfair competitive advantage" by not subscribing to EU social provisions or the euro.
Cheaper social charges would probably not impress companies like Toyota seeking to invest in Europe.
By contrast, they would be seriously put off by the prospect of being "on the wrong side of the biggest remaining barrier" to businesses in Europe, the single currency, Hughes predicted.
The Euro-MP also rejected British Prime Minister John Major's statement last week that signing the social chapter would result in half a million job losses in Britain.
A fair number of UK-based multinationals had voluntarily signed worker consultation agreements with the trade unions in spite of the British opt-out from the EU works council directive.
And the EU directive on parental leave provided for mothers or fathers to take unpaid time off.
"Where's the half a million jobs lost in that?" Hughes wondered.
As for potential new European social legislation, Hughes argued experience in the Netherlands showed that giving part time workers proper rights led to a surge in job creation, not job losses.
